Learn by Surprise, Commit by Proof

Kang-Sin Choi Affiliation: Ewha Womans University Email: kangsin@ewha.ac.kr
Abstract

We propose LSCP, a self-gated post-training framework for autonomous knowledge acquisition: learning only what a model does not already know, verified against what it does know, at a strength proportional to conviction, with no external oracle. When a passage produces anomalously high per-token loss, LSCP flags it, generates a Q&A chain that forces the model to articulate its own knowledge and identify gaps, then adjusts AdamW’s β2\beta_{2} proportionally to conviction depth kk (the number of self-verification steps the passage survives) via β2=0.999⋅rk\beta_{2}=0.999\cdot r^{k}. The entire learning intensity is governed by a single parameter rr. Beyond new knowledge, this process sharpens weakly encoded existing knowledge, which is a primary source of hallucination. The framework is self-extinguishing: as the model learns, per-token loss on learned passages decreases toward the surprisal threshold and the system progressively converges to standard AdamW. This models biological memory consolidation: temporary information in the context window is selectively consolidated into parametric weights, the model’s long-term memory. Experiments on the reference model (Qwen3-14B) and across six models (8B–32B, four families) show that standard fine-tuning produces rote memorization (perturbation gap (the ratio of paraphrase to original perplexity) of 11.6±0.2×11.6\pm 0.2\times baseline) while all LSCP conditions learn semantically (2.72.7–3.0×3.0\times). The r=1.0r=1.0 condition (identical optimizer, nearly identical data, only Q&A format differs) confirms that the training data format, not β2\beta_{2} gating, is the primary mechanism preventing memorization; gating instead protects neighboring knowledge from contamination by corrupt content (93±7%93\pm 7\% accuracy on adjacent questions at r=0.98r=0.98 vs. 90%90\% baseline).

1 Introduction

Can language models study by themselves? Modern large language models are trained to predict the next token in a sequence, an objective that, when applied to trillions of tokens, yields models with remarkable breadth of factual knowledge and reasoning ability. Yet once deployed, these models cannot learn from what they read. New information enters the context window and is discarded when the context ends. The model does not study; it merely consults a temporary buffer.

Existing approaches avoid rather than solve this problem. Fine-tuning forces weight updates indiscriminately, causing catastrophic forgetting [1]: the model learns new content but overwrites old knowledge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [2] avoids weight updates entirely, placing retrieved information in the context window, a short-term memory solution that never consolidates into long-term storage, with well-documented failure modes: context pollution [3], lost-in-the-middle degradation [4] and inability to form cross-document inferences. Knowledge editing techniques modify individual facts but do not scale. Continual learning methods address forgetting but require external supervision. None of these approaches consults the model’s own knowledge state to decide what should and should not be learned.

The core difficulty is that novelty is indistinguishable from noise. Why not simply amplify the learning signal for surprising content? Because high loss does not distinguish genuine novelty from noise. A groundbreaking scientific discovery and a plausible fabrication produce equally high per-token surprisal. Any mechanism that opens the optimizer to high-loss content without verification would corrupt the model’s weights.

Moreover, for the knowledge that matters most (cutting-edge discoveries, recent experimental results, findings not yet in any knowledge base), no external verification exists. Other models do not know it either; retrieval has nothing to retrieve; verifiable rewards cannot be computed for claims whose truth is not yet established. The only available reference is the model’s own existing knowledge: “does this new claim contradict what I already know?” This is not a limitation but a necessary design point. It is also exactly how humans evaluate cutting-edge knowledge: when peer review is unavailable, a scientist judges a new finding by its consistency with established principles. Imperfect, but the only option when external oracles do not exist.

There is a structural irony: the more a model has learned, the harder it becomes to learn anything new. AdamW [5] maintains a second-moment estimate vtv_{t} (controlled by β2≈0.999\beta_{2}\approx 0.999) that divides each gradient by the square root of its own historical variance. After trillions of training tokens, vtv_{t} is large and stable. When a novel passage produces a large gradient, vtv_{t} suppresses the update: the optimizer treats surprise as instability and applies the brakes precisely when the signal is strongest. We call this the Variance Lock. One might lower β2\beta_{2} to open it, but doing so indiscriminately would amplify noise along with novelty. The key challenge is selective lock release: opening the optimizer only for content that has been verified as consistent with existing knowledge.

Human memory solves this problem through a dedicated consolidation mechanism: the amygdala detects cognitively salient events [6], precisely those that are surprising or contradictory to prior beliefs, and gates their transfer from working memory to long-term storage via the hippocampus. We propose LSCP (Learn by Surprise, Commit by Proof), a self-gated post-training framework and computational analogue of this architecture, built on a simple observation: every language model already “notices” surprising content. The per-token loss

st=−log⁡pθ​(xt∣x<t)s_{t}=-\log p_{\theta}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}) (1)

is computed at every forward pass and is identical to the per-token cross-entropy loss used during training. When a passage produces anomalously high mean surprisal, the model is surprised. In cognitive neuroscience, surprise plays an analogous role: predictive coding theories [7, 8] hold that neural systems constantly predict upcoming input, and prediction error triggers both larger learning signals and the marking of new episodic events [9]. In current LLM architectures, this signal is used to compute a gradient and then discarded. LSCP provides the missing response:

The per-token loss is a free signal: already computed, already informative. It only needs a downstream pipeline to turn surprise into action: self-generated validation and gated weight updates.

The pipeline has three stages. Stage 1 detects surprise: passages with anomalously high per-token loss are flagged as candidates. Stage 2 verifies: a progressive chain of question-answer pairs tests whether the surprising content is consistent with the model’s existing knowledge, separating novelty from noise. Stage 3 opens the lock: for verified content, AdamW’s β2\beta_{2} is temporarily lowered in proportion to conviction depth, allowing the optimizer to absorb the new information; unverified content receives high β2\beta_{2}, keeping the lock closed. The result is selective transfer from context (short-term memory) to weights (long-term memory), gated by the model’s own epistemic state, with no external oracle. Algorithm 1 summarizes the pipeline.

2 Method

LSCP operates in three stages given a pretrained model MθM_{\theta} and an incoming document DD: (1) surprise: identifying passages the model does not already know, (2) self-verification: progressive Q&A generation and consistency checking and (3) consolidation: gated weight modification. Figure 1 provides an overview. We describe each stage in turn.

2.1 Stage 1: Detect and Ground

The connection between per-token loss and knowledge is direct: the LAMA probes [10] demonstrated that pretrained models store relational knowledge in their weights, and the feed-forward layers of Transformers can be interpreted as key-value memories [11] where frequently reinforced patterns are stored reliably and rare knowledge weakly or not at all. High surprisal on a passage therefore signals a gap in the model’s parametric knowledge.

Let D=(x1,x2,…,xT)D=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{T}) be a document tokenized into TT tokens. Aggregate per-token surprisal sts_{t} (defined in Section 1) over a sliding window of ww tokens to obtain passage-level surprisal:

Si=1w​∑t=i​w(i+1)​w−1st.S_{i}=\frac{1}{w}\sum_{t=iw}^{(i+1)w-1}s_{t}. (2)

A passage PiP_{i} is flagged as surprising if Si>μ+λ​σS_{i}>\mu+\lambda\sigma, where μ\mu and σ\sigma are the mean and standard deviation of surprisal computed over a large reference corpus, and λ\lambda is a threshold hyperparameter. Passages below this threshold are presumed to be covered adequately by existing weights and are not processed further. At this stage, the flag indicates only that the model’s predictions are poor for this passage; it does not distinguish novel content from corrupt content.

For each flagged passage, LSCP records a contextual grounding from signals that are already available from the forward pass:

Gi=(Pi,Si,di),G_{i}=\bigl(P_{i},\ S_{i},\ d_{i}\bigr), (3)

where PiP_{i} is the passage text, SiS_{i} is the passage-level mean surprisal retained as an importance weight, and did_{i} is the drop ratio, the normalized decrease in surprisal from the first third to the last third of the passage, measuring how much the model adapts to the content within the forward pass itself. Both numeric fields are derived from the single forward pass at zero additional generation cost. When source metadata is available (journal name, author credentials and document type), it is prepended to the passage text during training. This serves two purposes. First, situational context helps the model evaluate information: the same claim carries different weight from a peer-reviewed journal versus an anonymous post, just as a human reader’s judgment depends on where and how information is encountered. In non-linguistic learning, this principle is even more direct: knowing where you are and what you are looking at is inseparable from understanding what you perceive. Second, co-learning facts with their provenance provides source attribution as a byproduct: the model can later recall not just what it learned but where it learned it.

Two additional signals are available but not included in the formal grounding. Peaks, tokens whose individual surprisal sts_{t} exceeds a local threshold (e.g., the top decile), pinpoint where in the passage the model’s beliefs are under tension. When processing long documents, peak positions define the source window: the passage segment centered on the highest-surprisal region, trimmed to a manageable length for Stage 2. In our experiments, passages are short enough that the source window covers the full text. Narrative context, surrounding passages, document metadata, source credibility signals, provides situational information for Q&A generation but is not formalized as a grounding field because its availability varies across document types.

This mirrors the human cognitive experience of encountering unfamiliar information: the model “notices” a passage because it assigns low probability to it, exactly as a reader pauses at an unexpected claim. Actual conflict analysis, determining why the model’s beliefs are challenged and whether the challenge is valid, is deferred to Stage 2, where it belongs.

Critically, the grounding stores a pointer to the content rather than a copy. The storage overhead is thus proportional to the number of novel passages, not to document length.

In practice, many documents lack explicit source credibility signals: anonymous posts, scraped web text and OCR output. The grounding remains functional: SiS_{i} and did_{i} are always available from the forward pass, and Stage 2’s verification process provides the definitive filter regardless of metadata quality.

2.2 Stage 2: Verify, Grade and Annotate

An important clarification before describing the mechanism: Stage 2 does not verify whether a passage is true. It verifies whether a passage is consistent with the model’s existing knowledge. A model with systematically wrong beliefs will validate errors that fit those beliefs. The defense against this is not in Stage 2’s filtering accuracy but in Stage 3’s conviction-proportional learning: passages with shallow verification (kk low) receive weak learning, limiting the damage from any single corrupt passage that slips through.

Stage 2’s purpose is not merely to accept or reject a passage. It is to force the model to articulate its own knowledge about the passage’s claims, so that verified Q&A pairs can serve as targeted training data that strengthens specific weak points in the model’s weights.

When the model generates a question like “Can protein X actually bind to receptor Y?” and answers “Yes, because X has a binding domain complementary to Y’s active site,” two things happen simultaneously: (1) the consistency check verifies whether this answer is correct, and (2) the Q&A pair itself becomes a training item that reinforces the correct association protein X→receptor Y binding\text{protein X}\to\text{receptor Y binding} in the model’s parameters. If this association was weak or uncertain before (the model “sort of knew” but could not reliably produce the correct answer), training on this pair directly strengthens the relevant weights.

The Q&A chain is therefore not just a filter; it is a knowledge elicitation mechanism that produces training data precisely targeted at the model’s own epistemic gaps. Each verified pair represents something the model can confirm but may not have strongly committed to its weights, exactly the kind of knowledge that benefits most from consolidation.

A language model’s knowledge is distributed across billions of parameters. Recent work on knowledge localization (knowledge neurons [11], activation probing, causal tracing and sparse autoencoder features) has made progress in reading specific facts directly from weights or hidden states. However, these methods require additional training (a probe classifier, an SAE, or labeled fact triples) specific to each model and domain. Moreover, they operate on atomic, structured facts (“X is the capital of Y”) and cannot answer the compound question Stage 2 needs: “Is this passage’s claim consistent with everything the model knows about this topic?” LSCP’s Q&A chain requires zero additional training: it works on any pretrained model, in any domain, immediately. The text interface is the only probe that uses the model’s full reasoning capacity rather than a narrow linear classifier.

2.2.1 Generating the Q&A Chain

For each flagged passage PiP_{i}, LSCP uses MθM_{\theta} itself to generate a sequence of NN question-answer pairs in a single inference call:

𝒬i={(q1,a1),(q2,a2),…,(qN,aN)},\mathcal{Q}_{i}=\bigl\{(q_{1},a_{1}),(q_{2},a_{2}),\ldots,(q_{N},a_{N})\bigr\}, (4)

where N=⌈Si⋅c⌉N=\lceil S_{i}\cdot c\rceil scales with the passage’s surprisal (cc is a scaling constant), more surprising content receives more questions. In practice, NN is clamped to a safe range (NminN_{\min} to NmaxN_{\max}) to prevent degenerate chains. Each question is tagged by its epistemic origin, flowing naturally from what the model already knows toward what requires the passage.

[existing]

Questions about established domain knowledge the passage assumes or builds on. These must be answerable without reading PiP_{i}, from the model’s existing weights alone. They establish a verified baseline.

[mechanism]

The critical category. Rather than asking whether a claim “fits existing knowledge,” a question that the model answers permissively for anything it has not explicitly seen contradicted, mechanism questions attack the specific causal steps the passage chains together. If the passage claims “A causes B which leads to C which enables D,” the prompt instructs the model to test each link separately:

  • •

    Does A actually cause B? (based on known science, not the passage)

  • •

    Does B lead to C? (or does B actually lead to the opposite of C?)

  • •

    Is D achievable through C? (or are there known physical/biological barriers?)

The key instruction is: “The field exists” is not sufficient: the specific mechanism must be plausible. This prevents the failure mode observed in early experiments where the model confirmed that “vaccines can have neuroprotective effects” (general truth) without checking whether “the flu vaccine reduces dementia by 20% through anti-inflammatory mechanisms” (specific, implausible claim). A corrupt passage whose individual components are scientifically valid but whose assembled claim is false can only be caught by testing the joints between components.

[implication]

Questions of the form “if the passage’s claims are true, what specific, testable consequences follow? Do those consequences conflict with anything known?” These test internal coherence. Questions whose only possible source is the passage itself (specific measurements, unique named results) are excluded entirely; they cannot be verified.

Tags are generated by the model alongside each question. Empirically, single-call generation preserves passage-level context: the model sees the full passage and generates questions sequentially, causing corrupt passages’ internal inconsistencies to surface naturally in the question ordering (Cohen’s d=0.67d=0.67 for single-call vs. d=0.001d=0.001 for three-call; see Section 3).

2.2.2 Consistency Checking

Each pair (qi,ai)(q_{i},a_{i}) is validated against the model’s existing knowledge using a unified prompt that adapts its evaluation criterion to the question’s tag:

valid​(qi,ai)=𝟏​[Mθ​(qi)​ is consistent with ​ai].\text{valid}(q_{i},a_{i})=\mathbf{1}\bigl[M_{\theta}(q_{i})\text{ is consistent with }a_{i}\bigr]. (5)

For [mechanism] questions, the primary discrimination category, the prompt evaluates rigorously whether the specific causal step is scientifically plausible, whether known physical or biological constraints would prevent it and whether the claimed magnitude or efficiency is realistic. Few-shot examples in the prompt demonstrate the expected level of specificity: a FAIL example shows the model rejecting a protein-mineral interaction claim by citing the lack of epitaxial matching at the atomic level, not by generic appeal to “insufficient evidence.”

Tag-aware break policy.

Failures carry different evidential weight:

  • •

    [existing] FAIL (lenient): The question may be poorly formed or the model may lack niche background. The pipeline records the failure and continues.

  • •

    [mechanism] FAIL (hard break): The primary corruption signal. The passage’s specific causal claim contradicts established science. The chain terminates immediately.

  • •

    [implication] FAIL (hard break): Either the passage’s internal logic is incoherent, or the model cannot yet follow the reasoning because prerequisite knowledge is missing. In both cases, the passage should not be consolidated. The chain terminates.

2.2.3 From Chain Outcome to β2\beta_{2}

The chain produces a single number kk: how many questions passed before the chain completed or broke. This kk feeds directly into the β2\beta_{2} schedule (Section 2.3), providing a continuous spectrum from no learning (k=0k=0) to strong commitment (kk large). The number of questions NN itself scales with surprisal SiS_{i}, so more surprising passages face longer chains.

Only Q&A pairs that passed consistency checking are added to the training corpus ℱ\mathcal{F}, with each pair carrying its conviction depth kk (the number of verification steps it survived). Passages where the chain breaks at step jj contribute all pairs up to j−1j-1; passages that complete the full chain contribute all NN pairs. Each pair in ℱ\mathcal{F} represents knowledge the model could verify but had not strongly committed to its weights, precisely the weakly encoded associations that benefit most from reinforcement. The conviction depth kk determines the per-item β2\beta_{2} in Stage 3: pairs verified through more steps receive stronger learning.

2.2.4 Strangeness: Learning at Epistemic Boundaries

When the chain breaks at step jj, the reasoning behind the failure is not discarded but transformed into an uncertainty-framed training item: “The passage claims X, but I am uncertain. [reasoning from the failed check]. I cannot confirm or rule this out.” This strangeness record is added to the training corpus with the conviction depth kk at the break point, receiving correspondingly weak learning through β2=0.999⋅rk\beta_{2}=0.999\cdot r^{k}. The model does not learn the uncertain claim as fact; it learns that uncertainty exists on this topic, strengthening the association between the topic and epistemic caution. This is a distinctive feature of graduated accept: rather than discarding everything at the break point, the model encodes a calibrated record of its own knowledge boundary.

AdamW and the role of β2\beta_{2}.

vt\displaystyle v_{t} =β2​vt−1+(1−β2)​gt2,
